description: Tasks for weeks to months after death. Focus: Work through the administrative backlog systematically. This is a marathon, not a sprint.

tasks.title: File life insurance claims
tasks.description: If you found policies, file claims now. You need: death certificate, policy number, claim form. Claims typically pay within 2-4 weeks of filing.
tasks.why_now: This gets money flowing. Life insurance doesn't go through probate—beneficiaries receive it directly.
tasks.why_it_matters: Life insurance provides funds that may be needed for funeral costs, ongoing support, or estate expenses. Claims that aren't filed don't get paid.
tips: Call the insurance company to request claim forms
Claims typically pay within 2-4 weeks of filing
Life insurance bypasses probate—beneficiaries receive directly
If you can't find a policy, check the state's unclaimed property database
Some policies have accidental death benefits—ask if they apply

tasks.title: Open probate (if required)
tasks.description: If there's a will with assets over state threshold, or no will, you may need to file with probate court. This gives you legal authority to act. Some states have simplified processes for small estates.
tasks.why_now: Without probate (if required), you can't legally access many accounts or sell property. Some assets don't require probate—an attorney can advise.
tasks.why_it_matters: Probate gives the executor legal authority to manage the estate—access accounts, pay debts, distribute assets. Without it, institutions won't work with you.
tips: Not all assets go through probate (joint accounts, beneficiary designations, trusts)
Small estates may qualify for simplified procedures—check your state's threshold
An estate attorney can advise if probate is needed
Filing probate yourself is possible but complex—consider an attorney
Probate typically takes 6-12 months, sometimes longer

tasks.title: Notify banks and financial institutions
tasks.description: With death certificate and proof you're executor: notify each bank, close or transfer accounts. Joint accounts usually transfer to surviving holder. Individual accounts may require probate.
tasks.why_now: Banks need to be notified to protect the estate. Some accounts (POD/TOD, joint) can transfer without probate.
tasks.why_it_matters: Banks freeze accounts when notified of death (to protect the estate). Joint accounts and POD/TOD accounts transfer directly. Individual accounts require executor authority.
documents_needed: Letters Testamentary or Letters of Administration (for executor access)
tips: Joint accounts transfer to surviving owner automatically
POD (payable on death) accounts transfer to named beneficiary
Individual accounts require probate authority to access
Ask about any automatic payments that will stop
Safe deposit boxes may require court order or executor authority

tasks.title: Claim retirement accounts
tasks.description: 401k, IRA, pension—each has beneficiary designations. Contact each institution with death certificate. Beneficiaries can claim directly—these don't go through probate.
tasks.why_now: Retirement accounts pass to named beneficiaries directly. Beneficiaries may have options about how to take distributions.
tasks.why_it_matters: Retirement accounts can be significant assets. Beneficiaries inherit directly (outside probate) but need to take action to claim them.
tips: Contact the employer's HR or the account custodian
Beneficiaries may have options: lump sum, transfer to IRA, or required distributions
Spouse beneficiaries have more flexible options than non-spouse
There are tax implications to how you take distributions—consider consulting a tax advisor
Don't forget about pensions—these may have survivor benefits

tasks.title: Notify credit bureaus
tasks.description: Send death certificate to Equifax, Experian, TransUnion. This prevents identity theft and stops credit offers. Request a credit report to find accounts you might not know about.
tasks.why_now: Identity theft of deceased persons is common. Flagging the account protects the estate.
tasks.why_it_matters: Deceased persons are targets for identity theft. Notifying bureaus puts a 'deceased' flag on their credit file and helps you discover accounts you may not know about.
documents_needed: Proof of relationship or executor status
tips: Request a credit report—it reveals accounts you might not know about
Send written notice with death certificate to each bureau
This stops pre-approved credit offers
Keep checking periodically for new fraudulent accounts

tasks.title: Cancel subscriptions and memberships
tasks.description: Streaming services, gym, magazines, anything on autopay. Check their bank/card statements to find recurring charges. Cancel to stop bleeding money.
tasks.why_now: Subscriptions keep charging until cancelled. The estate shouldn't pay for services no longer being used.
tasks.why_it_matters: Recurring charges add up. The estate shouldn't pay for Netflix, gym memberships, or magazine subscriptions that aren't being used.
tips: Check bank and credit card statements for recurring charges
Common subscriptions: streaming (Netflix, Hulu), newspapers, gyms, Amazon Prime
Some services will refund recent charges—ask
Cancel autopay through the bank if you can't reach the service
Keep a list of what you've cancelled
tasks.can_wait_message: This can wait a few weeks, but subscriptions keep charging until cancelled.

tasks.title: Forward mail
tasks.description: Forward their mail to you or surviving parent. This catches bills, statements, and important notices you might miss.
tasks.why_now: Mail reveals accounts and bills you don't know about. It also prevents important notices from going unread.
tasks.why_it_matters: Mail forwarding helps you discover accounts, catch bills, and receive important legal notices. It also prevents mail from piling up at an empty home.
tips: Forward mail at usps.com or your local post office
Consider forwarding for 6-12 months to catch everything
Watch for bills, statements, and notices from unknown companies
Some first-class mail won't forward—check the original address periodically
Ask neighbors to collect any packages

tasks.title: Deal with property
tasks.description: If they owned a home: decide keep/sell, handle mortgage, transfer title (usually requires probate), manage maintenance meanwhile. No rush—make decisions when ready.
tasks.why_now: Property needs ongoing maintenance and insurance. But major decisions (sell/keep) can wait until you're ready.
tasks.why_it_matters: Real estate is often the largest estate asset. The property needs maintenance and insurance, but decisions about what to do with it don't have to be rushed.
documents_needed: Probate authority (usually needed to transfer title)
tips: Keep paying mortgage and insurance to protect the asset
Get the property appraised for estate value purposes
Transfer title usually requires probate—an attorney can help
Don't rush to sell—make decisions when you're ready
Consider an estate sale for contents if selling
tasks.can_wait_message: Major decisions can wait. Just keep up insurance and basic maintenance.

tasks.title: File final tax return
tasks.description: Their final return covers Jan 1 to death date. Due by the April deadline. Estate may also need a separate return if it generated income. A CPA can help.
tasks.why_now: This is a legal requirement. The estate cannot be fully settled until taxes are resolved.
tasks.why_it_matters: The final tax return is legally required. It may result in a refund or identify taxes owed. The estate may also need its own tax return if it earned income.
documents_needed: W-2s and 1099s for the year of death
Previous year's tax return for reference
Records of all income through date of death
tips: Write 'DECEASED' and the date of death across the top of Form 1040
A surviving spouse can file jointly for the year of death
File for an extension if you need more time (Form 4868)
Consider hiring a CPA experienced with estate taxes
The estate may need its own tax return (Form 1041) if it earned income
tasks.can_wait_message: You have until the April deadline (or can file for extension).

tasks.title: Distribute belongings and close estate
tasks.description: When accounts are settled and debts paid, distribute remaining assets per the will (or state law if no will). Sentimental items often take longer—that's okay.
tasks.why_now: This can only happen after debts are paid and probate (if needed) allows distribution.
tasks.why_it_matters: This is the final step—honoring your loved one's wishes (or following state law) in distributing what remains. Closure for the legal process.
tips: Get receipts or releases from beneficiaries for each distribution
Personal items with sentimental value can be the hardest—take your time
Consider a family meeting to discuss personal items
Keep some reserve for unexpected final expenses or taxes
Keep records of everything distributed
tasks.can_wait_message: This is the final step and will take months. No need to rush.
